Chelonia mydas: Adults graze seagrass and algae. The "green" comes from the colour of their body fat, not their shell.
Rhincodon typus: The largest fish alive, and a gentle filter feeder. Every whale shark's spot pattern is unique, so researchers identify individuals from divers' photos.
Octopus vulgaris: Three hearts, blue copper-based blood, and skin that changes colour and texture in a fraction of a second.
Mobula birostris: Wingspans reach about 7 m. Mantas queue at reef cleaning stations so small wrasses can pick parasites off them.
Amphiprion ocellaris: Every clownfish hatches male. The biggest fish in the anemone becomes the female, and if she dies, the dominant male changes sex to replace her.
Gymnothorax javanicus: That open-mouth stare isn't a threat, it's breathing. Morays also have a second set of jaws in the throat that shoots forward to grab prey.
Chromodoris annae: Nudibranchs are hermaphrodites, and the two "horns" (rhinophores) are smell and taste organs. The bright colours warn predators off.
Synchiropus splendidus: One of very few animals with true blue pigment in its cells. Mandarinfish pair up and spawn at dusk, a classic night-dive sighting.
Hippocampus kuda: The male carries the eggs in a brood pouch and gives birth to the young.
Pterois volitans: Venomous spines and almost no predators outside its home range. Since the 1980s it has spread invasively through the Caribbean and western Atlantic.
Ascarosepion latimanus: Hunts by rippling bands of colour across its body, seemingly mesmerising prey. The internal cuttlebone works like a buoyancy compensator.
Tursiops truncatus: Each dolphin develops a signature whistle that works much like a name, and others use it to call that individual.
Sphyrna lewini: Schools by the hundred at sites like Cocos and the Galápagos by day, then hunts alone at night. Listed as Critically Endangered.
Antennarius commerson: Waves a fleshy lure on its head to bait fish, then swallows them in a few milliseconds, one of the fastest strikes in the sea.
Cheilinus undulatus: Can grow to about 2 m and live 30+ years. Many start life female and switch to male later. Listed as Endangered.
Tridacna gigas: The largest bivalve, topping 200 kg. Algae living in its colourful mantle make much of its food from sunlight.
Carcharodon carcharias: Keeps parts of its body warmer than the surrounding water, which lets it hunt fast in cold seas.
Galeocerdo cuvier: Famous for eating almost anything; stomachs have turned up licence plates and tyres. The stripes fade as it grows.
Triaenodon obesus: Rests in caves by day, and unlike many sharks it can pump water over its gills while lying still. At night it hunts in packs, wedging into crevices.
Carcharhinus melanopterus: Patrols shallow reef flats, sometimes in water so shallow its black-tipped dorsal fin sticks out above the surface.
Stegostoma tigrinum: Juveniles are striped and adults are spotted, hence the confusing name. Captive females have had pups without a male.
Orectolobus maculatus: A carpet shark with a fringe of skin flaps around its mouth that breaks up its outline. It lies still on the bottom and ambushes passing fish.
Mola mola: Among the heaviest bony fish, with big adults topping a tonne. It often lies sideways at the surface, warming up after deep dives.
Taeniura lymma: The electric blue spots warn of venomous tail spines. It rides the rising tide into shallow sand flats to feed.
Aetobatus narinari: Digs clams out of the sand with its duck-bill snout and crushes them with plate-like teeth. Sometimes leaps clear out of the water.
Eretmochelys imbricata: A sponge specialist, eating prey that is toxic to most animals. Its shell was the main source of "tortoiseshell". Critically Endangered.
Dermochelys coriacea: The largest turtle, with a leathery back instead of a hard shell. It dives beyond 1,000 m and lives mostly on jellyfish.
Caretta caretta: Hatchlings read Earth's magnetic field to navigate across whole ocean basins. Massive jaws crush crabs and conchs.
Megaptera novaeangliae: Males sing long, complex songs that change over the season and spread from one population to another.
Orcinus orca: The largest member of the dolphin family. Different pods have their own vocal dialects.
Dugong dugon: The only strictly marine herbivorous mammal, grazing seagrass meadows. Likely behind some sailors' mermaid stories.
Trichechus manatus: Its closest living relatives are elephants. Worn molars are pushed out and replaced from the back throughout its life.
Zalophus californianus: Ear flaps and rear flippers that rotate forward let sea lions walk on land, unlike true seals. Famously playful with divers.
Enhydra lutris: Has the densest fur of any animal, up to a million hairs per square inch, and uses rocks as tools to crack shellfish.
Hapalochlaena lunulata: The rings flash bright blue when it's threatened. Its bite carries tetrodotoxin and can kill a person, though it's shy.
Thaumoctopus mimicus: Impersonates lionfish, flatfish and sea snakes. It was only discovered, off Sulawesi, in 1998.
Ascarosepion pfefferi: Walks along the bottom on its arms instead of swimming. Its flesh is reported to be toxic, and the colours advertise it.
Sepioteuthis lessoniana: Its fins run nearly the length of its body, so it's often mistaken for a cuttlefish. Most live less than a year.
Odontodactylus scyllarus: Its clubs strike with the acceleration of a small-calibre bullet, smashing shells. Its eyes have 16 types of photoreceptor, 12 of them for colour.
Stenopus hispidus: Lives in pairs and runs a cleaning station, waving long white antennae to advertise to passing fish.
Lysmata amboinensis: Groupers and morays open their mouths for it to pick out parasites. Hold out a hand and it may give you a manicure.
Hymenocera picta: Eats only starfish, flipping them over and feeding on them alive for days.
Acanthaster solaris: A coral-eating starfish covered in venomous spines. Population outbreaks can strip whole reefs of living coral.
Linckia laevigata: Can regrow an entire new star from a single arm.
Aurelia aurita: No brain, heart or bones. The four rings you can see through the bell are its reproductive organs.
Physalia physalis: Not a jellyfish but a colony of specialised organisms. The gas float works like a sail.
Phyllopteryx taeniolatus: Males carry the eggs stuck to the underside of the tail, with no pouch. Found only along southern Australia.
Phycodurus eques: The leafy appendages are camouflage, not fins; it moves with nearly transparent fins. The marine emblem of South Australia.
Hippocampus bargibanti: Under 2.5 cm and lives on a single sea fan whose colour and bumps it matches. It was discovered when a sea fan was collected for a museum.
Synanceia verrucosa: The most venomous fish known, with 13 venomous dorsal spines. It looks exactly like a lump of rock.
Diodon holocanthus: Inflates by swallowing water, raising its spines. Its teeth are fused into a beak for crunching shells.
Ostracion meleagris: Its body is a box of fused bony plates, and it releases toxin from its skin when stressed.
Balistoides conspicillum: Can lock its first dorsal spine upright to wedge itself into a crevice. The second spine is the "trigger" that unlocks it.
Rhinecanthus aculeatus: Grunts when alarmed and locks itself into holes with its dorsal spine. Named for the abstract face paint.
Labroides dimidiatus: Runs cleaning stations visited by fish of all sizes. In a 2019 study it appeared to recognise itself in a mirror.
Bolbometopon muricatum: The largest parrotfish, ramming coral with its head. One fish can turn about five tonnes of coral into sand a year.
Zanclus cornutus: The only species in its family, trailing a long white dorsal streamer. It played Gill in Finding Nemo.
Paracanthurus hepatus: Better known as Dory. A scalpel-sharp spine hides at the base of the tail, which is where surgeonfish get their name.
Pomacanthus imperator: Juveniles wear rings of blue and white that look nothing like the adult's yellow stripes.
Forcipiger flavissimus: Picks tiny invertebrates out of cracks with its long snout. The fake eyespot near the tail confuses predators.
Pterapogon kauderni: Males brood the eggs and then the young in their mouth. Found wild only around the Banggai Islands and listed as Endangered.
Rhinomuraena quaesita: Juveniles are black, become blue males, and turn yellow as females.
Heteroconger hassi: Colonies stay half-buried in sand, swaying to catch plankton, and vanish into their burrows when a diver gets close.
Caranx ignobilis: Has been filmed leaping out of the water to catch seabirds in flight.
Sphyraena barracuda: An ambush hunter that strikes in short bursts over 40 km/h. Often shadows divers out of curiosity.
Epinephelus lanceolatus: The largest bony fish on coral reefs, up to 2.7 m. Swallows prey whole, including small sharks and young turtles.
Lactoria cornuta: Two horns, a bony box for a body, and it blows jets of water to uncover prey in the sand.
Elysia crispata: Keeps the chloroplasts from the algae it eats alive inside its body. Whether it really photosynthesises with them is still debated.
Glaucus atlanticus: Floats upside down at the surface, eats Portuguese man o' war, and stores their stinging cells for its own defence.
Spirobranchus giganteus: The colourful spirals are feathery gills. It snaps them back into its tube in a split second when disturbed.
Opistognathus aurifrons: Builds a burrow from rubble, and the male broods the eggs in his mouth.
Carcharhinus amblyrhynchos: When threatened, it arches its back, drops its fins and swims stiffly from side to side as a warning. Listed as Endangered.
Negaprion brevirostris: Genetic tests at Bimini showed females come back to the island where they were born to have their own pups, 14 to 17 years later.
Carcharhinus longimanus: Has been seen swimming with pilot whales in the open ocean, likely because both hunt squid. Listed as Critically Endangered.
Ginglymostoma cirratum: Sucks prey out of holes with some of the strongest suction measured in any water-dwelling animal with a backbone.
Prionace glauca: One of the most fertile sharks. A single female can give birth to more than 100 pups in one litter.
Cetorhinus maximus: Cruises with its huge mouth wide open. A 5 m shark can filter about 450 tonnes of seawater an hour for tiny plankton.
Heterodontus portusjacksoni: Lays corkscrew-shaped egg cases, and the mother is thought to screw each soft case into a rock crevice with her mouth.
Triakis semifasciata: On summer days, groups of adult females gather in warm shallow bays. The heat may help their unborn pups grow faster.
Alopias pelagicus: Hunts by whipping its long tail at schools of fish to stun them, then eats the stunned fish, sometimes several from a single slap.
Carcharias taurus: The biggest embryo in each womb eats its smaller siblings before birth, so a mother never has more than two pups at a time.
Notorynchus cepedianus: Sometimes hunts in packs, sneaking up on large prey together, and its diet includes seals.
Hypanus americanus: Uncovers prey buried in the sand by spraying jets of water from its mouth or flapping its fins hard to stir up the seabed.
Rhinoptera bonasus: Migrates in schools of up to 10,000 rays, which leave Florida's west coast for Mexico's Yucatán every autumn.
Torpedo marmorata: Ancient Greek and Roman doctors pressed live electric rays like this one against patients, using the shocks to treat headaches and gout.
Trygonorrhina fasciata: A diamond-shaped mark just behind its eyes is how divers tell it apart from its look-alike cousin, the southern fiddler ray.
Laticauda colubrina: Females are much bigger than males and hunt large conger eels in deeper water, while males hunt small morays in the shallows.
Hydrophis platurus: Drinks from layers of rainwater floating on the sea surface, and can go about six months without fresh water during the dry season.
Amblyrhynchus cristatus: When El Niño makes food scarce, some can shrink their body length by up to 20%, then grow back when the algae return.
Crocodylus porosus: Rides ocean currents to travel long distances. One tagged crocodile swam 590 km along the Australian coast in 25 days.
Balaenoptera musculus: A newborn calf gains about 90 kg a day on its mother's rich milk, roughly the weight of an adult person.
Physeter macrocephalus: Has the largest brain of any animal that has ever lived, about 7 kg, roughly five times heavier than a human brain.
Monodon monoceros: The tusk is a tooth that spirals out through the left side of the upper jaw. It can reach 3 m and is packed with nerve endings.
Delphinapterus leucas: Unlike most whales, it can turn its head from side to side, because the bones in its neck are not fused together.
Stenella frontalis: Calves are born with no spots. Speckles appear in their first few years and keep spreading as the dolphin grows older.
Grampus griseus: Its skin never regains colour where it is scarred, so after years of scrapes from other dolphins, older adults can look almost white.
Odobenus rosmarus: Its scientific name means tooth-walker, after the way it hooks its tusks onto the ice to haul itself out of the water.
Halichoerus grypus: Its scientific name means hook-nosed sea pig. Pups are born with a fluffy white coat, which they shed after about three weeks.
Hydrurga leptonyx: Famous for hunting penguins, it also eats krill, sieving them from the water through cheek teeth that lock together like a strainer.
Aptenodytes forsteri: Fathers balance the egg on their feet for about two months of Antarctic winter, going nearly four months without food in all.
Spheniscus demersus: Brays loudly like a donkey, which earned it the old name jackass penguin. Listed as Critically Endangered.
Fratercula arctica: Its bright orange beak is a breeding-season outfit. After summer it sheds the colourful outer plates, leaving a smaller, duller bill.
Enteroctopus dofleini: A mother guards her eggs for six months or more without ever leaving to eat, and she dies soon after they hatch.
Amphioctopus marginatus: Collects coconut shell halves and carries them around to build a shelter later, thought to be the first tool use seen in an invertebrate.
Wunderpus photogenicus: Every one has its own pattern of white markings, so researchers can track individuals from photos without ever touching them.
Nautilus pompilius: Has about 90 tentacles with no suckers, and grips food with a sticky glue instead. Gas and liquid in its shell's chambers keep it afloat.
Euprymna tasmanica: Glowing bacteria in a light organ hide its shadow at night. By day it hides in the sand under a coat of grains glued on with mucus.
Hexabranchus sanguineus: A tiny emperor shrimp often lives on it. It also packs its spiral pink-red egg ribbons with toxins taken from the sponges it eats.
Flabellinopsis iodinea: Its purple, red and orange colours all come from a single pigment, which appears in three slightly different forms.
Phyllidia varicosa: Oozes a milky slime loaded with chemicals taken from the sponges it eats. In one aquarium, the slime killed a lobster sharing its tank.
Nembrotha kubaryana: Feeds on sea squirts and uses their toxins to defend itself against predators. It can grow longer than 12 cm.
Aplysia dactylomela: Squirts purple ink when disturbed, and can swim by folding its skin flaps into a funnel and pushing water out behind it.
Cypraea tigris: Its shells turned up in the ruins of Pompeii, thousands of kilometres from the Indo-Pacific reefs where it lives.
Cyphoma gibbosum: The bright spots are not on its shell. They are on the living mantle that covers its plain shell while it grazes on sea fans and soft corals.
Aliger gigas: Moves in hops: it jabs a sharp, claw-like plate on its foot into the sand and vaults forward. Its eyes peer out on long stalks.
Charonia tritonis: Grows to about half a metre long and is one of the few animals that hunts adult crown-of-thorns starfish, the coral-eating pest.
Panulirus argus: In autumn, after the first big storms, they march to deeper water in single-file lines dozens long, each touching the lobster in front.
Homarus gammarus: Blue when alive, it only turns red when cooked. Heat breaks apart a protein that keeps its red pigment looking blue.
Macrocheira kaempferi: Its legs can span up to about 3.7 m from claw to claw, the widest of any arthropod. Young ones stick sponges on their shells as camouflage.
Neopetrolisthes maculatus: Its big claws aren't for catching food. It sweeps plankton from the water with feathery fans on its mouthparts while hiding in its anemone.
Lybia tessellata: Can't feed with its own tiny claws, so it uses the anemones it holds to catch food, and waves them at attackers as stinging pom-poms.
Zenopontonia rex: Rides around on sea cucumbers and sea slugs like a taxi, nibbling their slime and droppings and dodging to the far side if danger comes.
Thor amboinensis: Under 2 cm long, it walks with its tail cocked up over its back, swaying it from side to side, which earned its cheeky name.
Stenorhynchus seticornis: In Brazil it has been seen cleaning moray eels and squirrelfish, picking at fish that would normally happily eat a crab.
Grapsus grapsus: Young crabs are black to blend in with lava rock, turning red, pink or yellow as they grow. Agile and able to leap, they are very hard to catch.
Protoreaster nodosus: Tiny sea star shrimps often live on its knobbly back, sheltering there and blending in with its colours.
Pycnopodia helianthoides: Can have up to 24 arms, grow a metre across and chase prey at a metre a minute, but wasting disease killed most of them. Listed as Critically Endangered.
Pisaster ochraceus: The original keystone species. When a scientist removed it from a rocky shore in the 1960s, mussels took over and crowded out many other species.
Diadema setosum: The orange ring on top looks like an eye but surrounds its bottom. It has no eyes, yet it senses light all over its body and hides from bright sun.
Heterocentrotus mamillatus: Its thick, blunt spines were once used to write on slate boards, just like pencils, which is how it got its name.
Toxopneustes pileolus: Named the most dangerous sea urchin by Guinness World Records. Its flower-like pincers inject venom that can cause severe pain and paralysis.
Bohadschia argus: Pearlfish live inside it, slipping in and out through its bottom. One study found 15 of them sharing a single sea cucumber.
Pseudocolochirus violaceus: When threatened it can gulp so much seawater that it nearly doubles in size, then lets the current carry it off to safety.
Astrophyton muricatum: Curls into a tight ball by day. At night it unfurls a net of branching arms nearly a metre wide, and rolls back up if you shine a light on it.
Chrysaora fuscescens: Young crabs hitch rides on its frilly arms and may nibble the jelly as they go. Those arms can trail up to about 4.5 m behind it.
Cyanea capillata: One found off Massachusetts in the 1800s reportedly had tentacles about 36 m long, longer than a blue whale, though some doubt the record.
Cassiopea andromeda: Lies on the seabed mouth-up so the algae in its tissues get sunlight. It reached the Mediterranean from the Red Sea through the Suez Canal.
Cotylorhiza tuberculata: Its sting barely affects people, and small fish often shelter among its frilly arms, using it as a floating hiding place.
Velella velella: Each one is a colony of tiny animals, not a single jelly. Its sail tilts left or right, so winds can send neighbours to opposite coasts.
Mastigias papua: In Palau's Jellyfish Lake, huge swarms follow the sun across the lake each day, turning as they swim, probably to give their algae even light.
Diploria labyrinthiformis: Grows upwards only about 3.5 mm a year, yet domes reach 2 m across. A fast-spreading coral disease has it listed as Critically Endangered.
Acropora palmata: Branches can grow 5 to 10 cm a year, yet about 97% of it vanished from Caribbean reefs between 1980 and 2006. Listed as Critically Endangered.
Gorgonia ventalina: Grows flat and side-on to the current like a net, catching drifting plankton, and can stand more than 1.5 m tall.
Plerogyra sinuosa: Its grape-like bubbles swell by day to give the algae inside more light, then shrink at night as tentacles reach out to catch food.
Corallium rubrum: Its branches thicken by only about 0.2 mm a year. People have prized its red skeleton for jewellery since ancient Egypt.
Fungia fungites: Starts life stuck to the reef, then breaks free as it grows and lives loose on the sand, usually as one big polyp up to 30 cm across.
Radianthus magnifica: Hosts about a dozen different clownfish species. It can also clone itself by splitting down the middle into two anemones.
Anthopleura xanthogrammica: Gets much of its green from tiny algae living in its tissues. Those growing in shady caves have few algae and look much paler.
Metridium senile: As it glides slowly along, it leaves scraps of its foot behind, and each scrap can grow into a brand new anemone.
Anemonia viridis: In southern Spain it's battered and deep-fried as a dish called ortiguillas. Its green colour comes partly from a glowing protein.
Cerianthus membranaceus: Lives in a tough tube it builds from mucus, sand and sticky threads fired from its skin. Some have lived at Naples Aquarium for over 50 years.
Xestospongia muta: Some are estimated to be over 2,000 years old, which is why it is called the redwood of the reef.
Clavelina moluccensis: Each blue bottle is under 2.5 cm long. Like all sea squirts, it starts life as a swimming tadpole, a clue that it's a distant cousin of ours.
Hermodice carunculata: If touched, its white bristles flare and break off in your skin, causing a burning pain that can last for hours.
Sabellastarte spectabilis: Its feathery crown is both net and gills, catching food and taking in oxygen. If stressed, it can shed the crown and grow a new one in weeks.
Mnemiopsis leidyi: Has no permanent bottom. A hole opens only when it needs to poo, about once an hour in adults, then seals up and disappears again.
Pseudobiceros bedfordi: Swims fast by rippling its ruffled edges, so it seems to fly over the reef like a magic carpet. It grows to about 8 to 10 cm long.
Holacanthus ciliaris: Young ones run cleaning stations, picking parasites off bigger fish. Adults switch to a diet made up mostly of sponges.
Pomacanthus paru: Lives in faithful pairs that guard a territory. Young ones run cleaning stations, and in the Caribbean even young green turtles visit them.
Pygoplites diacanthus: Feeds mainly on sponges and sea squirts and is often found near caves. Pairs spawn at dusk or after dark, after a spiralling dance.
Centropyge loriculus: Lives in harems of one male and several females. Fish from the Marquesas Islands have few or none of the black bars that the rest have.
Holacanthus passer: Young ones, and sometimes adults, work as cleaners, picking parasites off hammerhead sharks and manta rays. It also eats other fish's droppings.
Chaetodon auriga: In the Red Sea it lacks the black spot on the back fin that fish elsewhere carry, so Red Sea fish count as a separate subspecies.
Chaetodon lunula: Mostly active at night, when it hunts sea slugs, tubeworm tentacles and other small animals. It is usually seen in pairs or small groups.
Chaetodon capistratus: Pairs form young and seem to stay together for life. A false eye near its tail is easier to see than its real eyes, which may fool predators.
Chaetodon semilarvatus: Pairs often hover motionless for long periods under ledges of plate coral. It lives mainly in the Red Sea and the nearby Gulf of Aden.
Chelmon rostratus: The dark eyespot on its back fin stands out more than its real eye, which may fool predators. Its long, thin snout plucks worms from the reef.
Hypsypops rubicundus: Can live 57 years, the record for any damselfish. Males farm a patch of red algae as a nest, and females prefer nests already holding fresh eggs.
Abudefduf saxatilis: Males guard patches of reddish eggs for about a week, turning bluish while on duty. Young ones also pick parasites off green sea turtles.
Dascyllus aruanus: Lives in groups above one branching coral, ranked by size, with the biggest fish eating first. At any sign of danger they dive into the branches.
Amphiprion perideraion: Sometimes shares its anemone with other kinds of clownfish, such as Clark's anemonefish. Females grow to only about 10 cm.
Bodianus pulcher: Every one starts life female, and the biggest females later turn male. Its big canine teeth crunch sea urchins, which helps protect kelp forests.
Thalassoma bifasciatum: If the big blue-headed male disappears, the biggest female starts acting male within minutes to hours and fully changes sex in about 8 days.
Labrus mixtus: Starts life female, and the switch to a blue and orange male takes about seven months. Males build a dish-shaped nest from seaweed and guard the eggs.
Choerodon fasciatus: Has bright blue teeth, which it uses to crunch crabs, snails and shrimp. Some of its tuskfish relatives smash shells open on rocks.
Coris gaimard: Juveniles are bright red with big white spots and look nothing like the adults, which grow a bright yellow tail and hunt crabs and snails.
Achoerodus viridis: Starts life as a brown female and turns into a blue male once it reaches at least 60 cm. It has been the state fish of New South Wales since 1998.
Sparisoma viride: Scrapes algae off rock and dead coral with its beak-like teeth. The bits of coral it swallows get ground up and come out the other end as white sand.
Scarus guacamaia: One of the biggest parrotfish in the world, reaching about 1.2 m and 20 kg. Young ones grow up mostly among mangrove roots.
Sparisoma cretense: Unusually for a parrotfish, the females are the colourful ones, red with a yellow spot near the tail, while the males are plain grey.
Epinephelus marginatus: Every one starts adult life female, most turning male around age 12. It can live 50 years, and in no-fishing reserves even big adults come into the shallows.
Cephalopholis miniata: Lives in harems of one male and up to 12 females. About 80% of its food is small fish, which it ambushes with a sudden rush from the reef.
Lutjanus kasmira: Not native to Hawaii. It was released there in the late 1950s to boost fishing and has since spread along the whole island chain.
Ocyurus chrysurus: Anglers in Florida call the big ones flags, after their long, forked yellow tails. Divers on the Florida Keys reefs see them all the time.
Plectorhinchus chaetodonoides: Juveniles swim head-down, wildly flapping their fins, which may help them pass as toxic flatworms. Adults swap the white blotches for dark spots.
Anisotremus virginicus: Young ones work as cleaners, picking parasites off other fish. Like all grunts, it makes a grunting sound by grinding its teeth together.
Amblyeleotris wheeleri: Shares a burrow with a pistol shrimp that does all the digging. The shrimp can barely see, so it keeps an antenna on the goby, which quivers as a warning.
Nemateleotris magnifica: Hovers just above the sand facing into the current, flicking its long front fin as a signal. Pairs share a burrow and vanish into it when threatened.
Parablennius gattorugine: Each one has its own pattern of face markings, so researchers can tell individuals apart. Males guard the eggs for about a month until they hatch.
Ophioblennius macclurei: Clings to the reef with specially shaped fins, guarding its own patch of algae all day. At night it hides away inside the reef.
Neoclinus blanchardi: Rivals settle fights by pressing their huge open mouths together. It often makes its home in an empty shell, a bottle or even a drinks can.
Anarrhichthys ocellatus: Not a true eel. Pairs mate for life and share a cave, guarding a ball of up to 10,000 eggs, with only one parent leaving at a time to feed.
Taenianotus triacanthus: Sheds its whole skin every couple of weeks and can change colour afterwards. It rocks gently from side to side like a drifting dead leaf.
Cymbacephalus beauforti: Lacy flaps on its eyes break up the outline of its dark pupils, so even its eyes vanish as it lies flat on the reef waiting for prey.
Dactylopterus volitans: Despite its name it cannot fly. It walks along the seabed on its fins and can spread huge blue-edged wing-like fins, probably to startle predators.
Scorpaena scrofa: Grows to about 50 cm and has venomous spines, yet it is a classic ingredient of bouillabaisse, the famous fish stew of Marseille.
Gymnothorax funebris: Its green colour comes from a protective layer of slime over darker skin. At up to 2.5 m long, it is the biggest moray of the tropical Atlantic.
Gymnomuraena zebra: Instead of the fang-like teeth of most morays, it has flat, pebble-like teeth for crushing crabs, clams and sea urchins.
Muraena helena: Ancient Romans prized it as food and raised it in seaside fishponds. By day it hides in rocky cracks, coming out at night to hunt fish, crabs and octopuses.
Conger conger: Males and females spawn just once and then die. Before they swim off to spawn, their skeletons lighten and their teeth fall out.
Myrichthys colubrinus: Harmless, but its black and white bands copy the venomous banded sea krait. When prey hides deep in the sand, it digs in with its tail.
Arothron meleagris: Feeds mainly by biting the tips off branching corals. Most are dark with white spots, but some are bright yellow, often with a few black spots.
Arothron mappa: Can grow to 65 cm and usually lives alone near deep drop-offs. Like all pufferfish, its four beak-like teeth keep growing throughout its life.
Canthigaster valentini: Its skin carries a strong poison, so predators leave it alone. A harmless filefish copies its colour pattern to get the same protection.
Aluterus scriptus: Can grow to about 1.1 m long, and its colours shift quickly to match the background. Young ones drift across the open ocean under floating weed.
Oxymonacanthus longirostris: Eats almost nothing but Acropora coral and absorbs the coral's chemicals, so it smells like coral and is harder for predators to find.
Ostracion cubicum: Inspired a 2005 Mercedes-Benz concept car, though later studies found its boxy body is actually unstable, which is what makes it so nimble.
Balistoides viridescens: Guards a cone-shaped zone above its nest and may attack divers who enter it. Swim away sideways, not upwards, to get out of the cone.
Balistes vetula: Blows jets of water at spiny sea urchins to flip them over, then attacks the underside, where the spines are shortest.
Odonus niger: Its red teeth show even when its mouth is shut. When scared, it dives into a reef hole and locks itself in place with its dorsal spine.
Balistapus undulatus: One of the few fish that regularly eats spiny sea urchins. In East African marine parks it eats more burrowing urchins than any other predator.
Antennarius striatus: Wiggles a lure tipped with up to seven worm-like tails, then sucks in prey in about six thousandths of a second. It can swallow fish as big as itself.
Histrio histrio: Clambers through floating seaweed using its arm-like fins. It is so greedy that one was found with 16 young sargassumfish in its stomach.
Prionurus laticlavius: Starts life almost all yellow, then turns grey as it grows up, keeping only its bright yellow tail.
Solenostomus paradoxus: Unlike seahorses and pipefish, where males carry the young, the female carries up to about 350 eggs in a pouch made from her fused fins.
Dunckerocampus dactyliophorus: Like all pipefish, the male carries the eggs, in a pouch under his tail. Look for it alone or in pairs in caves and under ledges.
Aulostomus maculatus: Sneaks up on prey by swimming close beside bigger fish such as parrotfish, then sucks it in with a mouth that opens as wide as its body.
Aeoliscus strigatus: Swims head-down in tight, synchronised groups, and hides among the long spines of sea urchins when threatened.
Pseudanthias squamipinnis: Every one starts life female. A male keeps a harem of five to ten females, and if he dies, the top female turns into the new male.
Oxycirrhites typus: The only hawkfish with a long, tweezer-like snout. It perches on sea fans and black coral on steep walls, snapping up tiny crustaceans.
Gramma loreto: Keeps its belly towards the nearest surface, so it swims upside down under ledges. It also picks parasites off other fish.
Eques punctatus: Juveniles trail an extremely long dorsal fin that shrinks as they grow. Adults hide under ledges by day and hunt crustaceans at night.
Bothus lunatus: Both eyes sit on its left side and swivel separately. If one eye gets covered by sand, it struggles to match its colour to the seabed.
Platax teira: Tiny juveniles are brown and drift like floating leaves. Adults can switch from silvery white to dark-banded brown while you watch.
Zebrasoma flavescens: Can live for over 40 years in the wild. At night its bright yellow fades and a white band appears along its side.
Acanthurus leucosternon: Instead of flicking its head sideways to tear off algae like some tangs, it uses a hinge inside its lower jaw, which may help it graze in strong surge.
Echeneis naucrates: Its sucker is a heavily modified dorsal fin. It uses it to hitch rides on sharks, turtles, whales, ships and even scuba divers.
Sula nebouxii: Foot colour shows how well fed a bird is. Hungry birds' feet quickly turn duller, and females prefer males with brighter feet.
Pelecanus occidentalis: DDT once made its eggshells so thin that it was listed as endangered in the US. It recovered and came off the list in 2009.
Squatina squatina: Gone from most of a range that once ran from Norway to North Africa, leaving the Canary Islands as its last stronghold. Listed as Critically Endangered.
Poroderma africanum: Hides among squid egg beds and lunges at females arriving to lay. It can also tear the arms off octopuses by twisting its body.
Taeniurops meyeni: Can grow 1.8 m across and weigh about 150 kg, making it one of the biggest stingrays on the reef. Listed as Vulnerable.
Dardanus megistos: Scientists have watched it fold up its old outer skeleton after moulting and bury it in the sand, something no other crustacean is known to do.
Achaeus japonicus: Its body is only about 2 cm across, and its arms are covered in reddish hairs that trap bits of debris for extra camouflage.
Lauriea siagiani: Smaller than your fingernail, this pink and purple squat lobster lives on giant barrel sponges and is nicknamed the fairy crab.
Scyllarides latus: Has no claws and no spines, so it relies on thick armour and a strong grip on rocks. It comes out at night to eat molluscs such as limpets.
Thalassoma pavo: Buries itself in sand at night by shaking its tail hard. Warming seas seem to be helping it spread further north in the Mediterranean.
Echinaster sepositus: Its skin feels soapy and is dotted with tiny pits. It pushes small, deep red gills out through them to breathe.
Ophiothrix fragilis: Gathers in beds of up to 2,000 per square metre, each one raising an arm into the current to catch drifting food.
Ctenoides ales: Its flashing lips don't make light. They're lined with tiny silica spheres that reflect it, which may help scare off predators.
Plotosus lineatus: Juveniles pack into dense, ball-shaped schools of about 100 fish. The spines on their fins are highly venomous.
Acanthurus sohal: Fiercely guards its own patch of algae on the wave-washed reef edge and chases off intruders. Like all surgeonfish, it has a sharp blade by its tail.
Clione limacina: Seizes sea butterfly snails with six grabbing cones on its head, then pulls them out of their shells. It can survive nearly a year without food.
Corynactis viridis: Not a true anemone. It multiplies by splitting in half, so each patch on a rock wall is a group of clones, all the same colour.
Alcyonium digitatum: Spawns in the cold of December and January, and a colony can live for more than 20 years. Most colonies are either all male or all female.
Uranoscopus scaber: Buries itself with only its eyes showing, then wiggles a flap of skin on its lower jaw like bait to lure fish within reach.
